question: Let \(\boxed{N}\) mean the number of whole number divisors of \(N.\) For example, \(\boxed{3}=2\) because \(3\) has two divisors, \(1\) and \(3.\) Find the value of \[\boxed{\boxed{11}\times\boxed{20}}.\]
solution:
Each box asks for the number of positive whole-number divisors of its entry, so evaluate the inner boxes first. Factor pairs let us list the divisors without repeating them.

For \(11\), the only factor pair is \(1\cdot11\). For \(20\), the factor pairs are
\[
1\cdot20,\qquad 2\cdot10,\qquad 4\cdot5.
\]
These lists are complete: a factor pair for \(11\) must have a smaller member among \(1,2,3\), and a pair for \(20\) must have a smaller member among \(1,2,3,4\). Checking those candidates gives exactly the pairs above. Thus
\[
\boxed{11}=2,\qquad \boxed{20}=6.
\]
The entry in the outer box is therefore \(2\cdot6=12\). Its factor pairs are
\[
1\cdot12,\qquad 2\cdot6,\qquad 3\cdot4.
\]
Every pair for \(12\) has a smaller member at most \(3\), so this list is also complete. It gives the six distinct divisors \(1,2,3,4,6,12\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\boxed{11}\times\boxed{20}}=\boxed{12}=6.
\]
The answer is \(6\), choice A.
